periods.analysis: On-Time Performance closed 2024-Q3 at 73.5%, below the 80% target and in red, establishing the problem we need to manage quarter by quarter rather than explain away. With no prior-quarter comparison in this series, the baseline concern is clear: late inbound turns are stacking at Harborview International’s Concourse C hardstands, and the Port Connector taxiway work is adding minutes during the evening bank. Airfield Ops logged the heaviest slippage on routes tied to Gate C12-C18 and international widebody arrivals that missed tug windows. The airport remains safe and financially sound, but reliability is not where a coastal gateway city should accept it.
periods.recommendations: Stand up a daily 6:15 a.m. Turn Recovery huddle with Airfield Ops, the three largest carriers, TSA, and ground handlers focused on C-gate pushback readiness. Protect the remaining Port Connector work windows to overnight periods wherever safety allows, and publish a weekly variance report for Taxiways Kilo and Lima. Begin a red-status recovery track with named owners for gate availability, baggage make-up staffing, and first-wave aircraft servicing.

periods.analysis: On-Time Performance fell to 73% in 2024-Q4, down 0.5 points from 73.5%, so the red condition is not stabilizing yet. Holiday volumes amplified the weakness we saw in Q3, especially when late inbound aircraft from the Northeast missed Harborview’s 35-minute domestic turn plan. The new deicing pad dispatch protocol helped safety and sequencing, but it also exposed staffing gaps on Ramp Teams 4 and 7 during the 5 p.m. to 9 p.m. push. I am treating this as an operating-system failure, not a weather excuse.
periods.recommendations: Keep the Turn Recovery huddle in place and add a weekend irregular-operations captain with authority to reassign common-use gates B6-B10 within 15 minutes. Require each ground handler to submit a December-to-January corrective roster for tug drivers, belt loaders, and lavatory service crews. Use the airport’s carrier performance forum to set a shared target for recovering at least one point before summer construction impacts arrive.

periods.analysis: On-Time Performance moved from 73% to 72.4% in 2025-Q1, a further 0.6-point decline and still red. The winter schedule carried fewer passengers than Q4, so the drop tells me this is structural: aircraft are arriving late and we are not recovering the turn efficiently enough once they reach Harborview. The data team’s flight 410-series review showed recurring delay minutes at the international-to-domestic tow handoff near Stand I-3, and baggage sortation jams appeared twice on Pier 2 after early-morning diversions. The trend line is now three quarters long, and we need sharper operating discipline.
periods.recommendations: Launch a 45-day gate-turn audit on the 25 most delay-prone flights, with timestamps for chocks, bridge, first bag, last bag, fueling, catering, and pushback. Shift two cross-trained mechanics to the passenger boarding bridge quick-response cart for Concourse C through spring break. Direct the airport duty manager to escalate any tow-handoff delay over eight minutes to the Airport Operations Center in real time.

periods.analysis: On-Time Performance declined again in 2025-Q2 to 71.8%, down 0.6 points from 72.4%, keeping the measure firmly red. The summer ramp-up arrived before we had corrected the turn-time basics, and the Taxiway Lima shoulder rehabilitation narrowed our recovery margin during the afternoon cargo-passenger overlap. We did see better compliance with gate timestamping, which means the picture is clearer even if the outcome is worse. The most visible pinch points are now Gate C15, the west bag room feed, and late fueling calls on southbound leisure routes.
periods.recommendations: Move Taxiway Lima construction coordination into a twice-weekly constraint board with the contractor, Airfield Ops, cargo tenants, and airline station managers. Extend the gate-turn audit into a formal Reliability Recovery Sprint for C12-C18, with a named daily target for bridge availability and first-bag delivery. Add temporary fuel-truck staging on the south service road for the July schedule, subject to fire marshal clearance.

periods.analysis: On-Time Performance reached 71.5% in 2025-Q3, down 0.3 points from 71.8%, so the deterioration slowed but the status remains red. That smaller decline matters because the summer peak was heavy, but I will not call it progress until customers see more aircraft leaving on time. The C-gate sprint reduced some bridge delays, while thunderstorms and air-traffic flow programs on the Atlantic routes erased much of the gain. The chronic issue is still recovery: once the first wave slips, Harborview is carrying delay minutes deep into the evening bank.
periods.recommendations: Keep the C12-C18 Reliability Recovery Sprint active and extend it to B6-B10 for common-use flights before the holiday schedule is loaded. Pre-clear a thunderstorm playbook with the FAA tower, ramp control, and carriers that prioritizes rapid resequencing after ground stops. Begin publishing a daily first-wave departure scorecard to station managers, because the first 90 minutes are setting the whole day’s reliability.

periods.analysis: On-Time Performance dropped to 70.9% in 2025-Q4, down 0.6 points from 71.5%, returning us to the steeper red slide seen earlier in the arc. Holiday demand, coastal fog mornings, and uneven contractor coverage in the west bag room all contributed, but the result is still ours to manage. The first-wave scorecard showed better visibility, yet not enough corrective action before the noon and evening banks. At 70.9%, we are now nearly ten points under the target, and the reliability gap is affecting both passenger confidence and airline station planning.
periods.recommendations: Convert the Reliability Recovery Sprint into a 90-day executive recovery program chaired by the Aviation Director, with weekly carrier-by-carrier commitments. Require the west bag room vendor to provide surge staffing for peak holiday banks and a corrective maintenance log for belts WB-2 and WB-4. Freeze nonessential daytime airfield work during the two highest holiday travel weeks unless safety requires it.

periods.analysis: On-Time Performance fell to 70.4% in 2026-Q1, down 0.5 points from 70.9%, and remains red. The executive recovery program is producing better issue logs, but the operating result has not turned, which means we are still diagnosing faster than we are fixing. Winter crosswinds and FAA spacing contributed, but our controllable delays remain concentrated in aircraft servicing, baggage induction, and gate release discipline. I am concerned, but the problem is now bounded enough to manage with tighter accountability.
periods.recommendations: Move from weekly commitments to daily exception management for any carrier or handler missing the turn standard on three consecutive banks. Add a temporary second ramp-control coordinator from 2 p.m. to 10 p.m. to reduce gate-release lag during irregular operations. Tie vendor invoices for baggage and ground handling to documented staffing coverage and response times at the problem assets and gates.

periods.analysis: On-Time Performance ended 2026-Q2 at 70%, down 0.4 points from 70.4%, marking the eighth red quarter in this sequence. The decline is slightly less severe than the prior quarter, but 70% is not acceptable for Harborview’s role as the region’s airport and seaport gateway. Construction phasing on the north apron, heavier cruise-airport transfer days, and continued first-wave misses kept pressure on the system even as the new ramp-control coordinator reduced some gate-release lag. The arc is clear: we have improved visibility and contained some failure points, but we have not yet produced the turnaround residents, passengers, and carriers need.
periods.recommendations: Set a formal 2026-Q3 recovery threshold with monthly milestones toward returning above 74% before pushing for the 80% target. Extend the second ramp-control coordinator through the summer and add a cruise-transfer operating plan for Fridays through Sundays with the seaport shuttle vendors and airline stations. Bring the north apron construction phasing, gate allocations, and handler staffing plan to the Aviation & Seaport performance review for decision, not discussion.

periods.analysis: On-time performance improved from 70% to 72%, but remains eight percentage points below the 80% target. The improvement does not yet resolve the first-wave and gate-sequencing problems identified last quarter.
periods.recommendations: Review first-wave departures, north apron phasing and handler coverage with carriers; assign a dated recovery plan rather than treating the two-point gain as a turnaround.
